key_points.point: The document argues that safety net healthcare systems, which serve marginalized populations, are currently disadvantaged by a lack of accessible, low-resource tools for bias mitigation. By providing open-source code and a 'Supplementary Playbook,' the authors aim to democratize access to these tools, preventing safety net patients from falling behind the innovation curve. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of ensuring that transformative technologies are widely accessible rather than monopolized by well-resourced academic centers. The authors acknowledge that their methods are not a panacea, but rather a practical starting point for systems with limited resources.
key_points.verbatim: Without concrete, easy to implement pathways to identify and mitigate bias, safety net patients will continue to fall behind the innovation curve.

key_points.point: The authors advocate for the integration of predictive models into clinical workflows to augment human judgment, viewing this as a necessary evolution in healthcare. They emphasize that the goal is not to halt AI adoption, but to ensure equity during its deployment so that all patients can reap the benefits. This reflects an accelerationist desire to harness AI's potential for improving diagnostic tasks and operational efficiency. The document notes that this requires proactive efforts to measure and mitigate bias rather than avoiding the technology entirely.
key_points.verbatim: We are on the precipice of an AI and machine learning revolution in healthcare. Algorithms are increasingly augmenting human judgement in diagnostic tasks like cancer identification and prediction of inpatient sepsis while assuming responsibility for repetitive tasks like allocating appointments, staffing, and hospital beds.

key_points.point: The document asserts that algorithmic bias, where model performance varies across sociodemographic classes, directly exacerbates systemic healthcare disparities. By using metrics like Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD) to measure false negative rates, the authors demonstrate that models can preferentially allocate resources based on class membership rather than clinical need. This supports the safetyist belief that implicit biases in AI can lead to real-world discriminatory outcomes. The authors highlight that even models with fair global performance can exhibit significant bias when run locally on specific patient populations.
key_points.verbatim: Algorithmic bias occurs when predictive model performance varies meaningfully across sociodemographic classes, exacerbating systemic healthcare disparities.

key_points.point: The authors emphasize the need for standardized, transparent reporting and evaluation methods for AI models in healthcare to strengthen patient trust. They argue that as predictive models are integrated into clinical applications, minimizing bias is essential for maintaining public confidence, especially given that trust in health systems is at an all-time low. This aligns with the safetyist desire for institutionalized transparency and accountability in AI development. The document notes that patients are increasingly concerned about receiving misdiagnoses from decision-support tools.
key_points.verbatim: As predictive models are integrated across clinical applications, transparently minimizing algorithmic bias in every healthcare system is essential for strengthening trust in medicine.

key_points.point: The document provides empirical evidence of documented harms caused by existing AI systems, specifically in healthcare settings like opioid misuse prediction and skin cancer detection. It highlights that these biases are not merely theoretical but have measurable impacts on historically underserved patients. This aligns with the skeptic focus on identifying and documenting present, measurable harms. The authors acknowledge that bias is multifactorial and can be introduced at any stage of the algorithmic lifecycle, including data collection and feature selection.
key_points.verbatim: Bias has been identified in algorithms predicting or measuring opioid misuse, healthcare cost and utilization, hypoxemia, and skin cancer, among others.

key_points.point: The authors advocate for rigorous, systematic methods to assess and audit AI models for bias at the health system level, rather than relying on national performance metrics. They demonstrate that local performance can differ significantly from nationally representative samples, necessitating local evaluation. This supports the skeptic intention of mandating algorithmic accountability through local auditing. The document notes that many healthcare systems currently lack the expertise and resources to perform these evaluations, which is a significant barrier to equity.
key_points.verbatim: Healthcare systems may see biased local performance even if overall performance is unbiased. An algorithm which performs well on a nationally representative sample may offer biased predictions when run locally on patient populations with different demographic, clinical, and social characteristics.

factual_claims.claim: NYC Health + Hospitals serves more than 1 million New Yorkers, 90% of whom are patients of color and 70% of whom are covered by Medicaid or lack insurance.
In a 2023 Pew survey, 60% of Americans reported feeling uncomfortable about the idea of AI influencing diagnostic decisions.

unmapped_concepts.suggested_description: A strategy within safetyist and skeptic discourse that prioritizes computationally efficient, post-processing methods for bias mitigation in resource-constrained healthcare settings. It focuses on methods like threshold adjustment that do not require access to original training data or high-level machine learning expertise.
unmapped_concepts.concept: The document tests threshold adjustment and reject option classification as scalable, low-resource approaches to bias mitigation. It finds that threshold adjustment is more effective and easier to implement for safety net systems than in-processing or pre-processing methods.
